country.lede: What is Switzerland’s central bank dealing with right now, and what will it most likely do at its next decision? This page explains it from the very beginning, in everyday language, one step at a time. You do not need any background in money or economics.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the SNB policy rate where it is, at 0.00%. A small rise to 0.25% remains a possibility given robust growth, but inflation inside the target zone makes waiting the most sensible path.
verdict.confidence_note: The decision is nearly seven weeks away, with important consumer price reports and oil price movements still ahead before December 10.
verdict.short_version: Inflation sits comfortably at 1.0% inside the SNB’s 0%–2% target zone, and the SNB's conditional forecast shows price stability continuing. With growth solid and the franc slightly weaker, a hold is most likely, though a small rate rise cannot be entirely ruled out.
verdict.card_why: Inflation sits at 1.0% inside the SNB's target zone, keeping a rate hold as the most likely outcome for December.
verdict.last_move: Cut to 0% on Jun 19, 2025; held five times since (latest Sep 24, 2026)

why_steps.title: The SNB has one main job, and two tools
why_steps.html: The SNB’s main job is to keep prices stable while taking account of how the economy is doing. It defines stable prices in an unusual way: a rise in consumer prices of less than 2% a year, and not falling either. In practice that is a comfort zone of 0% to 2% (SNB presentation, Oct 7). Unlike most central banks, there is no single 2% bull’s-eye: anything in the zone counts as success. Its first tool is the SNB policy rate, which steers what banks charge each other for overnight loans (that market rate is called SARON, short for Swiss Average Rate Overnight, and many Swiss mortgages follow it). Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get dearer, people and firms borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today the rate is 0.00%, where it has been since June 2025. Its second tool is special to Switzerland: foreign exchange interventions. The SNB can create francs and use them to buy euros or dollars. That makes the franc a bit weaker, which makes imports dearer and nudges Swiss prices up. In its words, interventions are used “as necessary to complement the SNB’s interest rate policy” (SNB). So the SNB has two pedals for the gas, and it can also go below zero: from 2015 to 2022 its rate was negative, as low as −0.75%, which means banks paid to park money at the SNB.

why_steps.title: Prices are rising, but only gently
why_steps.html: Consumer prices (the CPI, or Consumer Price Index, measured by the Federal Statistical Office, FSO) were 1.0% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 0.8% in August (FSO data via Trading Economics; SNB). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost CHF 100 a year ago now costs about CHF 101. In the U.S. or Canada, by comparison, prices are up about 3% to 3.5% a year (see their monitors). The “core” rate, which leaves out the jumpiest prices such as fuel and fresh food, was only 0.5% in September. Why so low? Oil products make up only about 2% of the Swiss shopping basket, according to SNB Governing Board member Petra Tschudin (“Erdölprodukte machen nur 2% aus”, interview), so an oil shock hits Swiss prices far less than elsewhere. A strong franc has also kept imported goods cheap for years, and food prices are still falling (−1.0% in a year).

why_steps.title: The SNB’s own forecast says “no need to move”
why_steps.html: Four times a year the SNB publishes a conditional inflation forecast: what it thinks inflation will be over the next three years if the rate stays where it is. If that line stays inside the 0%–2% zone, the rate is “about right”. If it heads above 2%, the SNB brakes; if it heads below 0%, it presses the gas. In September, with the rate at 0%, the forecast was 0.7% on average for 2026, 0.8% for 2027 and 0.8% for 2028, a little higher than in June (0.6%, 0.6%, 0.7%). The quarterly table in the SNB’s bulletin peaks at about 1.2% around the turn of the year (Quarterly Bulletin 3/2026). The SNB concluded: “Our monetary policy is appropriate to keep inflation within the range consistent with price stability.” (introductory remarks). For a rise in December, that forecast would need to move up a lot.

why_steps.title: The economy is stronger than expected, and the franc is weaker
why_steps.html: Swiss output (GDP, the value of everything the country produces) grew 1.5% in April–June, “the strongest GDP growth recorded since the third quarter of 2021” (SECO). Much of it came from chemicals and pharmaceuticals (+10.5%), which swing a lot, but the SNB says growth was solid even without them. Forecasters raised their numbers: SECO’s expert group now expects 1.7% growth in 2026, while KOF expects 1.9% and the SNB expects 1.5% to 2% (SECO forecast). At the same time the franc lost some of its strength. Measured against a basket of trading partners, it fell 2.8% between mid-June and mid-September (SNB). A weaker franc helps exporters and makes imports dearer, which pushes Swiss inflation up a little. That is exactly the help the SNB wanted when it said in March and June that it was more willing to intervene against a strong franc. Today one euro costs about CHF 0.92 and one U.S. dollar about CHF 0.82 (Oct 22, SNB).

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: SNB raised its own forecast in September
Weaker franc adds to import prices
Fed and ECB rates higher; KOF expects an SNB rise
right: Forecast with 0% rate stays in range to 2028
Oil only ~2% of the Swiss basket
A rise could pull the franc up again

why_steps.html: The Raise side has more arguments than three months ago, and we take it seriously. What tips us toward Hold is the SNB’s own rule of thumb: it moves when its forecast leaves the 0%–2% zone, and in September it did not come close. A rise would also strengthen the franc, undoing the weakening that the SNB said is “having a supportive effect” on the economy. That is why we say about 70% Hold, 25% Raise and 5% Cut.

why_steps.title: What the SNB has been saying
why_steps.html: In every statement since June 2025 the decision sentence has been the same: “The Swiss National Bank is leaving the SNB policy rate unchanged at 0%.” What changed is the tone about the franc and the risks. In March and June 2026 the SNB said its willingness to intervene had increased, to counter “a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc” (March release). In September it was calmer: “Medium-term inflationary pressure has increased only slightly.” and “We will therefore continue to monitor the situation and adjust our monetary policy if necessary,” (September release; remarks). The SNB gives no hints about future moves on purpose. Petra Tschudin said in August: “Wir publizieren keine Zinsprognosen.” (“We do not publish interest-rate forecasts.”, interview). Outside the SNB, the KOF Swiss Economic Institute at ETH Zurich “expects the SNB to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points at its next monetary policy assessment” (KOF, Sep 30). A “basis point” is one-hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points means 0.25 points. That is a serious outside voice for Raise; it is not the SNB’s view.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: prices on November 3
why_steps.html: On Tuesday, November 3, at 8:30 a.m. Swiss time, the FSO publishes October’s consumer prices. On October 22 the SNB also published a summary of what the Governing Board discussed in September, showing the careful debate behind the decision. If headline inflation reaches about 1.5% or more and core inflation climbs to about 0.8% or more, a December rise becomes much more likely and Raise could become our main call. If inflation stays around 1% with core near 0.5%, Hold becomes even more likely. The November figures (early December) will be the last word before the decision.

timeline.title: The SNB cut its rate to 0%
timeline.what: The SNB lowered its rate by 0.25 points, from 0.25% to 0%, effective June 20, 2025. Banks’ deposits at the SNB above a set limit (the “threshold”) earn 0.25 points less, so in effect −0.25%.
timeline.why: Prices were actually falling: inflation was −0.1% in May 2025. The SNB pressed the gas to stop that. It said that without the cut its forecast would have been lower.
timeline.people: Savings accounts paid close to nothing. SARON-linked mortgages got a little cheaper.
timeline.because: the rate reached zero, and the SNB began to wait and see.

timeline.title: Held at 0% as U.S. tariffs bite
timeline.what: The SNB held at 0%. It said: “The economic outlook for Switzerland has deteriorated due to significantly higher US tariffs.” Inflation had risen slightly, to 0.2% in August 2025.
timeline.why: Tariffs (taxes on imports) made Swiss goods dearer for American buyers. Unemployment had risen and was likely to keep rising. But inflation was back above zero, so no new cut was needed.
timeline.people: Workers in export firms faced more uncertainty. Borrowing costs stayed very low.
timeline.because: the SNB kept watching trade and the franc, with its foot steady.

timeline.title: Held again: prices flat, tariffs lower
timeline.what: The SNB held at 0%. Inflation fell to 0.0% in November 2025. GDP had shrunk in July–September, mainly because of pharmaceuticals. The SNB said lower U.S. tariffs had slightly improved the outlook.
timeline.why: Zero inflation sits at the very bottom of the 0%–2% zone, but the SNB’s forecast (0.3% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027) stayed inside it, so it saw no need to go negative.
timeline.people: Prices in shops were the same as a year earlier on average. Hotels, rents and clothing got a little cheaper.
timeline.because: the SNB entered 2026 at 0%, with inflation at zero and a strong franc.

timeline.title: War in the Middle East; the SNB guards against a soaring franc
timeline.what: A war in the Middle East pushed up energy prices. On March 19 the SNB held at 0% and said its willingness to intervene in the currency market had increased: “The SNB thereby counters a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc”. Inflation was 0.1% in February.
timeline.why: In a crisis, investors around the world buy francs as a “safe haven”, like moving savings into a strong safe. A sudden jump in the franc would make imports much cheaper and could push Swiss prices back below zero.
timeline.people: Fuel and heating oil got dearer. Exporters and tourism worried about a stronger franc making Switzerland expensive for foreigners.
timeline.because: the SNB had two worries at once: dearer energy (prices up) and a stronger franc (prices down).

timeline.title: Energy lifts Swiss inflation, a little
timeline.what: Inflation rose from 0.1% in February to 0.6% in May, “mainly” because of oil products. The franc, adjusted for prices, peaked in March: the BIS real effective exchange rate index reached 103.80, then eased to 102.67 in May.
timeline.why: Oil products are only about 2% of the Swiss basket, so even a big oil jump adds only a few tenths of a point to Swiss inflation.
timeline.people: A basket that cost CHF 100 a year earlier now cost about CHF 100.60. Much less pain than in most other countries.
timeline.because: inflation was finally moving up inside the zone, which eased the risk of falling prices.

timeline.title: Held at 0%; a technical tweak to bank deposits
timeline.what: The SNB held at 0%, saying: “Inflation has risen in recent months as a result of higher energy prices.” It forecast 0.6% inflation for both 2026 and 2027 and about 1% growth for 2026. On June 22 it lowered the “threshold factor” for bank deposits from 15 to 13.5, from August 1.
timeline.why: The forecast stayed well inside the zone. The deposit change was technical: the SNB said it “has no impact on the current monetary policy stance”; it keeps the overnight market active.
timeline.people: Nothing changed for loans or savings. The SNB warned that “The upward pressure on the Swiss franc could also increase again.”
timeline.because: the SNB went into the summer still worried more about a strong franc than about high prices.

timeline.title: The franc weakens; the economy surprises
timeline.what: The franc fell 2.8% against trading partners (2.2% against the euro, 3.8% against the dollar) between mid-June and mid-September. On September 3 SECO reported GDP up 1.5% in April–June, the strongest since 2021. The 10-year bond rate rose from 0.39% in mid-June to 0.58% in mid-September.
timeline.why: Higher rates abroad make euro and dollar savings more attractive than franc savings, which pulls money out of the franc. Exports of medicines boosted growth.
timeline.people: Holidays abroad and imported goods got a little dearer. Fixed-rate mortgages edged up: the SNB puts the 10-year mortgage rate at about 2.0%.
timeline.because: the threat of a runaway franc faded, and forecasters started talking about higher, not lower, rates.

timeline.title: Neighbours brake; Swiss forecasts go up
timeline.what: The U.S. Fed raised its rate to 3.75%–4.00% on September 16, and the ECB’s deposit rate rose to 2.50% from the same day. On September 17 SECO’s expert group raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.7% (from 0.9%), with inflation of 0.6% in 2026 and 2027.
timeline.why: Abroad, the energy shock pushed inflation well above targets. In Switzerland it did not, which is why forecasters still saw low inflation.
timeline.people: The gap between Swiss and foreign interest rates grew, which tends to weaken the franc and helps exporters.
timeline.because: everyone watched whether the SNB would follow its neighbours.

timeline.title: Held at 0%, forecast nudged up
timeline.what: The SNB held. “Inflation rose slightly, from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August.” Goods prices rose for the first time since May 2024. The forecast rose to 0.7% (2026), 0.8% (2027) and 0.8% (2028). Growth was expected at 1.5% to 2% this year.
timeline.why: “Medium-term inflationary pressure has increased only slightly.” The forecast stayed inside the zone, so no need to brake. The SNB still said it is “willing to be active in the foreign exchange market” if needed.
timeline.people: No change for borrowers or savers. The SNB said the weaker franc and its low rate are “having a supportive effect” on the economy.
timeline.because: attention moved to the next price reports and to the oil price.

timeline.title: Calls for a rise, prices at 1%, policy discussion published
timeline.what: On September 30 KOF forecast a 0.25-point SNB rise. On October 1 FSO reported September inflation at 1.0% (core 0.5%). Brent oil hit US$135.51 on October 2, then US$125.44 on October 6. Unemployment held at 3.0% in September. On October 22 the SNB published its summary of monetary policy discussions.
timeline.because: our reading is “no rush, but a December rise is possible”, which is why our main call is Hold.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 0.00%
choices.meaning: the SNB keeps its foot where it is for a sixth meeting in a row. It would likely repeat that it is ready to act in the currency market and to “adjust our monetary policy if necessary”.
for: Inflation is inside the zone. 1.0% headline and 0.5% core in September, well below 2%.
The SNB’s forecast passes the test. With a 0% rate, inflation stays between 0.7% and 0.8% a year on average through 2028.
Oil matters less here. Oil products are only about 2% of the Swiss basket.
A rise could strengthen the franc again. That would undo the weakening the SNB called supportive.
The SNB said so itself. “Our monetary policy is appropriate to keep inflation within the range consistent with price stability.”
against: Inflation has climbed from 0.1% in February to 1.0% in September, the fastest pace since September 2024.
Growth is strong and forecasters raised their numbers sharply.
KOF expects a rise, and the 2-year bond rate suggests markets see some chance of higher rates.
choices.everyday: SARON mortgages, savings accounts and business loans would stay roughly where they are. Fixed-rate mortgages follow bond markets, so they could still move a little.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 0.25%
choices.meaning: the SNB presses the brake lightly for the first time since 2023, moving away from zero before inflation gets close to 2%.
for: Inflation is climbing. From 0.0% in November 2025 to 1.0% in September 2026, and the SNB expected a further rise in the last quarter.
The economy is strong. GDP up 1.5% in a single quarter; KOF now sees 1.9% growth in 2026.
Others are braking. The Fed and the ECB raised rates in September, which weakens the franc and lifts Swiss import prices.
Respected forecasters expect it. KOF forecasts a 0.25-point rise at the next assessment.
December brings a full new forecast. If oil stays high, that forecast could move up noticeably.
against: Even with a 0% rate, the SNB’s September forecast never comes near 2%.
Core inflation is only 0.5%; there is little sign of fuel costs spreading to other prices.
A rise would make the franc more attractive, which the SNB spent months trying to prevent.
choices.everyday: SARON mortgages and lines of credit would cost a little more; savings accounts might pay a little more. On a CHF 500,000 SARON mortgage, 0.25 points is about CHF 1,250 more a year (our arithmetic). The franc would probably firm up.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate below zero
choices.meaning: the SNB would go back to negative rates, pressing the gas to stop the franc soaring or prices falling.
for: Only if a sudden crisis (for example a worse Middle East war or a market crash) sent investors piling into the franc, pushing it sharply higher and inflation back toward zero.
The SNB has done it before: −0.75% from 2015, and it does not rule it out today.
against: Inflation is rising, not falling. A cut now would make no sense against a 1.0% inflation rate.
The SNB prefers currency interventions first. Tschudin noted that a cut below zero works “etwas anders” (somewhat differently) from a normal cut, because banks pass it on only partly.
choices.everyday: banks might charge large depositors fees again and mortgages would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise itself would signal a serious crisis.

change.lead: Our 70% / 25% / 5% guess is based on what we know today. Because the SNB decides only in December, a lot of new information will arrive first. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The SNB can only react to information it has already seen. Everything released before December 10 can change the December decision, and this time that is almost two months of data, including two inflation reports. A report released after it can only shape the next decision, on March 18, 2027. That is why most of the table below is marked “Before”.

producer_and_import_prices.why: An early warning of shop prices, and a direct read of how the weaker franc and oil feed into import costs.
producer_and_import_prices.trigger: Turning clearly positive (above about +1% a year) → small push toward Raise.

summary_of_monetary_policy_dis.why: The SNB gives no vote count, so this is the best window into whether a rise was already debated.
summary_of_monetary_policy_dis.trigger: Talk of a rise being “discussed” or of upside risks dominating → Raise up. Stress on franc strength → Hold firms up.

retail_sales.why: Shows whether households keep spending despite high fuel costs.

kof_economic_barometer.why: A quick read of business mood after the oil spike.
kof_economic_barometer.trigger: A sharp drop below 100 → Hold firms up; a further rise → Raise a little more likely.

consumer_price_index_cpi.why: The most important report this autumn. It will show whether the early-October oil spike is lifting Swiss prices.
consumer_price_index_cpi.trigger: Headline about 1.5% or more and core about 0.8% or more → Raise could become our top pick. Headline near 1% and core near 0.5% → more confident in Hold.

labour_market_situation.why: Shows whether the strong spring is turning into hiring, or whether unemployment keeps creeping up.
labour_market_situation.trigger: Seasonally adjusted rate falling to 3.0% or lower → leans Raise a little. Rising to 3.2% or more → leans Hold.

foreign_currency_reserves.why: Big changes can hint at currency interventions, though valuation moves also matter.
foreign_currency_reserves.trigger: Only a hint; affects our reading of the franc, not the odds directly.

gdp.why: Tells the SNB whether the economy is running hot or cooling after the pharma-driven spring.
gdp.trigger: Another strong quarter (above about 0.5%) → Raise up. A fall → Hold, and more so if unemployment rises too.

consumer_price_index_cpi_novem.why: Together with October, it decides whether the December forecast moves up a lot.
consumer_price_index_cpi_novem.trigger: Same thresholds as October. Two hot reports in a row would make a rise close to a coin flip or better.

economic_forecast_9_00_a_m.why: Too late for December, but shapes the outlook for 2027.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Brent oil jumped to US$135.51 on October 2 before easing to US$125.44 on October 6 (FRED). The SNB’s September forecast assumed Brent of about US$105 at the start, then gradually lower (SNB). If oil stays well above that, the December forecast will rise and so will the chance of a rise.

The franc. A renewed rush into the franc (a “safe haven” in a crisis) would push the SNB toward Hold and currency purchases, and could even revive talk of negative rates. A further slide in the franc would push toward Raise.
U.S. trade policy. SECO notes a U.S. investigation launched on March 11, 2026 that includes Switzerland; its outcome is unknown. New tariffs would hurt exports and make a hold more likely.

Speeches before December. Board members speak often; Petra Tschudin and Thomas Moser are listed for a money market event in Geneva on October 29 (SNB). Any hint that the forecast could leave the 0%–2% zone would matter.

report_card.one: Prices are 1.0% higher than a year ago, inside the SNB’s 0%–2% zone, but rising.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 1.0%), core inflation (0.5%), the SNB’s conditional forecast (0.7%–0.8% a year to 2028), producer and import prices, and inflation expectations (firms expect 1.0% over the next 6–12 months).
report_card.why: Inflation is comfortably inside the target zone even during a major oil shock, and expectations are low and stable. Unlike most countries on this site, Switzerland’s price problem is not “too high”. Watch-outs: it has climbed from 0.0% last November, and the SNB expects it to rise a bit further this quarter.
report_card.change: Headline above about 1.5% with core rising → yellow. A drop back to zero or below → yellow from the other side.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason we expect a hold. The SNB brakes when its forecast heads above 2%, and today it is far from that.

report_card.one: Unemployment is low by world standards (3.0%), but higher than a year ago.
report_card.look: Registered unemployment (SECO), job seekers, vacancies, short-time work, and the broader international (ILO) measure.
report_card.why: Registered unemployment is 3.0% and job seekers total 227,592, while vacancies stand at 44,199. The international measure was 5.1% in the second quarter. On the bright side, registered vacancies are up and firms told the SNB they plan to hire more. Wages are expected to rise about 1.5% this year, faster than prices.
report_card.change: Unemployment falling back below 3% → green. Rising above about 3.3% → red.
report_card.matters: A gently loosening job market means wages are not pushing prices up, which supports waiting.

report_card.one: A very strong spring, and forecasts have been raised.
report_card.look: GDP (adjusted for big sports events), retail sales, the KOF Economic Barometer, and forecasts from SECO, KOF and the SNB.
report_card.why: GDP grew 1.5% in April–June, the most since 2021. SECO now sees 1.7% growth for 2026, KOF 1.9%, the SNB 1.5% to 2%. Shop sales were up 3.2% on a year in August, and the KOF barometer rose to 109.1. Caveat: much of the spring boom was pharmaceuticals, which can reverse quickly, and the SNB says factory capacity use is still below average.
report_card.change: A weak third quarter (Nov 30) or a new tariff shock → yellow.
report_card.matters: Strong growth is the main reason a rise is on the table at all. If the economy keeps running this hot, the SNB may want to move off zero.

report_card.one: Market rates have risen a little, and the franc has eased from its highs.
report_card.look: The overnight rate SARON, Confederation (government) bond rates, the franc against the euro and dollar, and mortgage rates.
report_card.why: SARON (−0.06%) sits right where the SNB wants it, just under 0%. The 10-year Confederation bond yield is 0.525%, and the 2-year (0.20%) is above SARON, so markets expect somewhat higher rates. The franc fell 2.8% on a trade-weighted basis over the summer, which the SNB called supportive, but it is still very strong by long-run standards (one euro buys CHF 0.9211).
report_card.change: A sudden franc surge or a jump in bond rates → red. Calm markets → green.
report_card.matters: The franc is the SNB’s second pedal. As long as the franc stays calm, the SNB has room to wait; a surge would make a rise very unlikely.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) checks the prices of hundreds of everyday things, like food, rent, transport and clothes, and compares them with a year ago. A 1.0% rise means a CHF 100 shopping basket now costs about CHF 101.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: this is the number the SNB’s 0%–2% goal is based on. It is the fastest rise since September 2024, but still well inside the zone. October’s figure arrives on November 3.

core_inflation.what: CPI without the jumpiest items, such as energy and fresh food.
core_inflation.why: it shows the underlying trend. At 0.5%, there is little sign that expensive oil is spreading into other prices, which is the main argument for waiting.

cpi_inflation_earlier_in_2026.what: the path of inflation as quoted in the SNB’s three 2026 statements.
cpi_inflation_earlier_in_2026.why: inflation has climbed steadily from zero, “mainly” because of oil products. The direction, not the level, is what keeps a rise on the table.

snb_conditional_inflation_forecast.what: the SNB’s forecast of yearly average inflation if the rate stays at 0%. The quarterly path peaks at about 1.2% around the turn of the year.
snb_conditional_inflation_forecast.why: this is the SNB’s main decision tool. If it stays inside 0%–2%, the rate is judged “about right”. It edged up in September, partly because of the weaker franc.

transport_prices.what: the cost of getting around, including fuel, cars and travel.
transport_prices.why: this is where the oil shock shows up most. It was the biggest single push to inflation in September.

food_and_non_alcoholic_drinks.what: prices of groceries and soft drinks.
food_and_non_alcoholic_drinks.why: falling food prices offset much of the fuel shock for Swiss households, one reason Swiss inflation stays low.

producer_and_import_prices.what: prices that Swiss factories charge and that importers pay.
producer_and_import_prices.why: an early warning of shop prices. Still negative in August, but the weaker franc and oil could turn it positive.

firms_inflation_expectations.what: what Swiss companies told the SNB’s regional delegates they expect inflation to be.
firms_inflation_expectations.why: central banks fear that if people expect high inflation, it becomes self-fulfilling. Swiss expectations are low and steady.

oil_products_share_of_the_cpi_basket.what: “Erdölprodukte machen nur 2% aus.” (Oil products make up only 2%.)
oil_products_share_of_the_cpi_basket.why: this explains why the oil shock that pushed inflation to 3% or more elsewhere lifted Swiss inflation only to about 1%.

registered_unemployment_rate.what: the share of the workforce registered as unemployed at regional job centres.
registered_unemployment_rate.why: low by world standards at 3.0% in September.

unemployment_rate_seasonally_adjusted.what: the same rate with normal seasonal swings (such as construction in winter) removed.
unemployment_rate_seasonally_adjusted.why: it shows the trend. At 3.1% in September, it has stopped rising for now.

job_seekers.what: everyone registered as looking for work, including people in training schemes or with temporary jobs.
job_seekers.why: a broader view of slack in the job market.

registered_vacancies.what: open jobs reported to the regional job centres.
registered_vacancies.why: rising vacancies suggest firms are hiring again, which supports the strong-growth story.

unemployment_rate_international_ilo_me.what: unemployment measured by a survey using international rules, counting people who are not registered too.
unemployment_rate_international_ilo_me.why: at 5.1% in Q2 2026, it is higher than the registered rate and comparable with other countries.

short_time_work.what: workers whose hours were cut temporarily with state support instead of being laid off.
short_time_work.why: a crisis indicator with only 8,339 people affected in June.

wage_growth_company_talks.what: average pay rises that companies told the SNB about.
wage_growth_company_talks.why: wages rising about 1.5% in 2026 and 1.3% expected in 2027, meaning real incomes grow moderately.

gdp_growth_sport_adjusted.what: the total value of everything Switzerland produces, adjusted for the income from big international sports events held here.
gdp_growth_sport_adjusted.why: growth of +1.5% vs previous quarter in Q2 2026 is the main argument for a possible rate rise.

gdp_growth_vs_a_year_ago_sport_adjuste.what: output compared with the same quarter a year earlier.
gdp_growth_vs_a_year_ago_sport_adjuste.why: at +2.3% in Q2 2026, it confirms the economy is growing well above its usual pace.

private_consumption.why: spending by families grew +0.3% in Q2 2026; the boom came from exports, not shoppers.

goods_exports_excluding_valuables.what: goods sold abroad, without gold and other valuables.
goods_exports_excluding_valuables.why: up +5.5% vs previous quarter in Q2 2026. The weaker franc should help them further.

growth_forecasts_for_2026.what: what the government’s expert group, the KOF institute and the SNB expect for this year’s growth.
growth_forecasts_for_2026.why: SECO 1.7%; KOF 1.9%; SNB 1.5%–2%. A faster economy makes the SNB more open to a rise.

retail_sales.what: how much people spent in shops.
retail_sales.why: up +3.2% vs a year ago in August 2026. Households are still spending despite expensive fuel.

kof_economic_barometer.what: a survey-based indicator of where the Swiss economy is heading in the next months; around 100 is average.
kof_economic_barometer.why: at 109.1 in September 2026, the outlook for the Swiss economy remains favourable.

snb_policy_rate.what: the SNB’s main interest rate. It steers the rate at which banks lend to each other overnight.
snb_policy_rate.why: at 0.00% on October 22, 2026. The December 10 decision is about keeping it here, raising it, or cutting it.

rate_on_banks_deposits_above_the_thres.what: banks earn the policy rate on SNB deposits up to a limit, and −0.25% on anything above it.
rate_on_banks_deposits_above_the_thres.why: at −0.25% as of October 16, 2026, this keeps SARON close to the policy rate.

saron_overnight_rate.what: the Swiss Average Rate Overnight, the rate banks pay each other for one-day loans backed by securities.
saron_overnight_rate.why: at −0.06% on October 21, 2026, it shows the SNB’s rate is fully working in the market.

10_year_confederation_bond_yield.what: the interest rate the Swiss government pays to borrow for 10 years.
10_year_confederation_bond_yield.why: at 0.525% on October 22, 2026. Fixed-rate mortgages follow it.

2_year_confederation_bond_yield.what: the rate the government pays to borrow for 2 years.
2_year_confederation_bond_yield.why: at 0.20% on October 22, 2026, it is above SARON, a sign that investors see some chance of SNB rises.

euro_in_francs.what: how many francs one euro costs.
euro_in_francs.why: at CHF 0.9211 on October 22, 2026, a strong franc cheapens imports and lowers Swiss inflation.

u_s_dollar_in_francs.what: how many francs one U.S. dollar costs.
u_s_dollar_in_francs.why: at CHF 0.8199 on October 22, 2026. Oil is priced in dollars, so exchange rates affect fuel costs.

trade_weighted_franc.what: the franc against a basket of trading partners’ currencies.
trade_weighted_franc.why: down 2.8% from mid-June to mid-September 2026, supporting exports and import prices.

mortgage_rates.what: the cost of a 10-year fixed mortgage, and the official reference rate used to adjust rents.
mortgage_rates.why: about 2.0% for 10-year mortgages and 1.25% for the reference rate in September 2026.

oil_price_brent.what: the world benchmark price for crude oil.
oil_price_brent.why: at US$125.44 a barrel on October 6, 2026, remaining well above the SNB's baseline assumption.

snb_oil_assumption.what: the oil path the SNB built into its September forecast.
snb_oil_assumption.why: about US$105 at the start, then falling, which has been exceeded by current oil prices.

u_s_fed_rate.what: the U.S. central bank’s main rate.
u_s_fed_rate.why: at 3.75%–4.00% since September 16, 2026, making dollar savings more attractive.

ecb_deposit_rate.what: the euro area’s main interest rate.
ecb_deposit_rate.why: at 2.50% on October 22, 2026, helping keep the franc from rising too fast.

euro_area_growth_forecast_snb_assumpti.what: how fast the SNB expects Switzerland’s biggest export market to grow.
euro_area_growth_forecast_snb_assumpti.why: 0.8% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027, capping how far Swiss exports can carry the economy.

seco_view_of_the_main_risk.what: the main risk to the economic outlook.
seco_view_of_the_main_risk.why: Middle East conflict remains a major risk to global growth and energy prices.

w: What it said: Details on the September monetary policy assessment where the policy rate was left unchanged at 0%.
Why it matters: Confirms the depth of the Governing Board's deliberations on inflation and economic risks.
What it said: “Medium-term inflationary pressure has increased only slightly.” and the SNB is “willing to be active in the foreign exchange market” as necessary.
Why it matters: no signal of an imminent rise; the franc tool remains ready.

What it said: “We will therefore continue to monitor the situation and adjust our monetary policy if necessary,” and “Our monetary policy is appropriate to keep inflation within the range consistent with price stability.”
Why it matters: the SNB is comfortable today but keeps both doors open.

said.pv: June: pressure on the franc “could also increase again”
w: What it said: the medium-term forecast is slightly higher, “reflecting, among other things, the weakening of the Swiss franc.”
Why it matters: a weaker franc does some of the SNB’s work, which reduces the need to keep the gas pedal pressed (or to cut).
What it said: “Inflation has risen in recent months as a result of higher energy prices.” and “The upward pressure on the Swiss franc could also increase again.”
Why it matters: in June the main fear was a too-strong franc, not too-high inflation.
What it said: “The SNB thereby counters a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc”.
Why it matters: shows the SNB’s first line of defence against a safe-haven franc is currency intervention, not negative rates.
What it said: “We do not publish interest-rate forecasts.” She also said a cut below zero works “etwas anders” (somewhat differently) from a normal cut.
Why it matters: do not expect the SNB to pre-announce a December move. Surprises are possible.

said.n: KOF Swiss Economic Institute (not the SNB)
w: What it said: KOF “expects the SNB to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points at its next monetary policy assessment.”
Why it matters: a respected outside forecaster disagrees with our base case. It is the strongest single argument for our 25% Raise chance.

gaps: Official FSO inflation release for September. The FSO website blocked our reading tool, so the September CPI (1.0%), core (0.5%), the category details and the release dates come from Trading Economics, which reports FSO data. August (0.8%) is confirmed by the SNB. Why it matters: the headline number is very likely right, but we could not check the FSO’s own wording.

Market odds for December. We found no official source for market-implied chances (from SARON futures or swaps). The 2-year Confederation yield (0.20%) is from Trading Economics. Why it matters: we cannot compare our 25% chance of a rise with what markets price.

Currency interventions. We could not verify how much (if any) the SNB bought or sold in currency markets in 2026; its intervention figures are published with a delay. Why it matters: interventions are the SNB’s second pedal.

How we gathered data: data was gathered on October 22, 2026 with web tools, so every number was read directly from the page linked next to it (SNB, SECO, KOF, FRED, and Trading Economics where official FSO pages could not be opened).

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The SNB counts prices as stable when consumer prices rise by less than 2% a year and do not fall: a comfort zone of 0% to 2%. Unlike most countries on this site, Swiss inflation is low.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers tell us whether people can find work. The SNB has no jobs target, but a weaker job market usually means slower wage and price growth later.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing and whether people are spending. A hot economy can push prices up; a weak one pulls them down.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the SNB’s own rate and how markets are reacting. Mortgages, savings and the franc all depend on them.
group_intros.said: SNB officials do not give hints about future moves on purpose, but their words still show what they worry about. Reading them carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision.
group_intros.global: Switzerland is a small, open economy. What happens to oil, trade and other central banks matters a lot, and the franc reacts to global fear.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year and a bit, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every assessment the SNB has three options for its rate (and it can also act on the franc). Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date Swiss CPI series (its OECD copy stops in April 2025), and it has no SNB policy rate or SARON series, so for those use the FSO and the SNB directly. Several FRED series below are monthly or quarterly averages from the OECD, Eurostat or the BIS and arrive with a delay, so they may differ from our daily figures. Swiss GDP on FRED is measured in euros.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.
